headline: A doctor beat a billionaire for Ohio governor.
summary: Amy Acton beat Vivek Ramaswamy for Ohio governor, the first woman ever to win the job. Ohio went for Trump three times. Ramaswamy spent $4m on an ad in which Acton's estranged mother said she "lied her entire life"; Nikki Haley and Mike DeWine condemned it, Trump called it "powerful." Acton, a doctor, said "the healing begins today."

cover_question.q: Was it OK to use her mom in an ad?

cover_answer: No. It left out what she'd been through as a child.
table_question: Is anything off limits when you're trying to win?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: A doctor named Amy Acton got picked to be the boss of Ohio, a whole state. No woman has ever had that job there before. A state is big, like our town and every town for a day's drive put together, and the governor looks after all of it. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: A doctor, a job, a first. The ad never comes up: a seven-year-old can do nothing with it. At seven the size of a thing is the fact, so the day's drive does the work.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole thing, so the script gives them a doctor who got a big job, and the size of the job as a day's drive. The ad and what it left out stay off the table; Cantor's work says harm to a parent or child is what frightens this age most. Expect "can I be the boss of a state?" Yes.

8-12.script: Ohio voted for Trump three times, so most expected Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican, to win. The race was about prices, then his side spent $4m on an ad using Amy Acton's own mother against her. Nikki Haley called it wrong; Trump called it "powerful." The voters refereed, and picked Acton, a doctor.
8-12.why: An expected winner, an ad, a verdict. Fair is their call to make.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out rules and whether adults keep them, so the script hands them a chain: the expected result, the ad, and the vote as the referee. That Republicans split over the ad is the detail that matters: it shows the rule is not a team's. Expect "what did her mom say?" Quote it, and say she won anyway.

13-17.script: Ramaswamy's $4m ad has Acton's estranged mother saying she "lied her entire life." The BBC notes it omits that the mother's husband was charged with raping Acton as a child. Where is the line, and who draws it? Second: he now says he's "rooting" for her. Does that undo anything?
13-17.why: Two arguments: the line, then the concession. They go first. A fourteen-year-old can argue a line without being told where it is.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: her mother really said it, and the ad left out the fact that changes it. The script asks where the line is and who draws it, then whether a gracious concession repairs anything. Expect "would you run that ad to win?" Say what you would do.

5-7.a: No. People saw it and voted for her anyway.

8-12.q: Why did Ohio pick her if Ohio likes Trump?
8-12.a: The BBC says the race was about prices. Voters pick per job, like a ref per game.
Runs the state, like a principal runs a school.

13-17.q: Was it OK to use her mom in an ad?
13-17.a: No. It left out what she'd been through as a child.

13-17.q: Why did Trump like the ad?
13-17.a: He called it "powerful" and said keep it on. Vance said stop whining.
